result.summary: Troy despairs after Hector's and Penthesileia's deaths, and Memnon arrives with his Aethiopians. Next day he kills Antilochus and fights Achilles, who kills him. Dawn mourns, his body is carried away, and his comrades become birds.

scenes.title: Trojan council of despair
scenes.summary: Thymoetes, Priam and Polydamas debate fleeing, holding the walls, or returning Helen. Paris insults Polydamas.
scenes.stakes: Troy risks destruction by Achilles and the loss of its people.

scenes.title: Memnon feasted by Priam
scenes.summary: Memnon arrives and is welcomed with a banquet and the heirloom cup. He retires early to rest.
scenes.stakes: Memnon's last night before his death.

scenes.title: Zeus warns the gods
scenes.summary: Zeus forbids the gods to intervene in tomorrow's slaughter.
scenes.stakes: The gods must endure the deaths of their dear ones.

scenes.title: Memnon slays Antilochus
scenes.summary: Armies clash. Memnon kills Antilochus, spares old Nestor and routs the Argives.
scenes.stakes: Nestor risks death and the Argives face rout.

scenes.title: Achilles kills Memnon
scenes.summary: Nestor calls Achilles, who duels Memnon after boasts about their mothers. The Fates tip the balance and Achilles kills him.

scenes.title: Dawn mourns her son
scenes.summary: Winds carry Memnon's body to Aesopus' stream. Dawn grieves, threatens darkness, then yields to Zeus; the Aethiopians become birds.
scenes.stakes: Dawn's grief threatens to leave the world in darkness.

characters.name: Polydamas
characters.description: Prudent Trojan who urges returning Helen

characters.name: Helen
characters.description: Woman from Sparta over whom war is fought

characters.name: Tithonus
characters.description: Memnon's father, given immortality by Dawn

notable_quotes.reason: Nestor's saying that necessity gives even cowards courage.
Memnon laughs in the afterlife, a striking image of his fate.

analysis.text: Grief and fate: even gods must bow to Zeus's decree, and Dawn's mourning mirrors human loss.
The poem explains the birds called Memnons and a bloody river through aetiological myth.

legacy.text: The Memnonides birds and Memnon's tale drew later writers, and the Colossi of Memnon in Egypt were named after him.

fun_facts.text: This poem is by Quintus of Smyrna, a later continuation of the Iliad.

language_notes.text: "Aweless" means fearless, not inspiring awe; it is a stock epithet for Hector here.
Penthesileia was the Amazon queen who came to help Troy and was killed by Achilles in the preceding book.
"Meseemed" is archaic for "it seemed to me"; "hitherward" means toward this place.
Memnon, king of the Aethiopians, was an ally of Troy and son of Dawn; his arrival is the hope the whole scene turns on.
"I trow" means "I believe"; "sore" means grievous.
"Rede" means counsel or advice; "gainsay" means to contradict.
Helen was taken from Sparta by Paris; returning her with her treasure is the offer the Greeks originally demanded.
"I wot" means "I know."
Polydamas recalls that he had urged Hector to stay within the city instead of fighting; Hector refused and died.
"Battle-blencher" is a coined insult: one who flinches (blenches) from battle.
"Quotha" is archaic for "says he," used sarcastically to mock another's words.
"Caitiff" means a base, cowardly wretch.
"Wantwit" means a senseless, foolish person; here the adjective means foolish.
Aethiops: Ethiopians, here a dark-skinned people of the far east or south, Memnon's subjects.
"Eternal-wheeling Northern Wain": the Great Bear or Plough constellation, which never sets and so guided sailors.
Forspent: utterly exhausted. "Troyfolk" means the people of Troy.
Immortality given to his sire: Eos (the Dawn) won Tithonus, Memnon's father, unending life, though not unending youth.
Solymi: a warlike people of Asia Minor, met on Memnon's journey.
The cup's line of owners follows the Trojan royal house, from Dardanus down to Priam.
Cyprian Queen: Aphrodite (Venus), born or worshipped at Cyprus; she was given to Hephaestus as wife.
Unmeet: improper. "Fain" means gladly, "board" means table.
"Cronos' son, All-father" names Zeus by patronymic and title; "to-morn" means tomorrow, and "spake" means spoke.
Clasping the knees was the traditional gesture of a suppliant begging a favour; Zeus forbids it.
The "bright morning-star" and the "Child of Mists of Night" point to Memnon, son of Dawn (Eos), whose "last sleep" ends as he wakes for his final battle.
"Welkin" is an archaic word for the sky; "herdeth" means herds together.
"Strait" means narrow.
"Aethiop men" are Memnon's Ethiopian troops, allies of Troy.
Thryus lay by the river Alpheus in Nestor's realm of Pylos; these men had followed Nestor to Troy.
"Morion" is a helmet; the translator uses it for the Trojan-side warrior's headgear.
Periclymenus, a Pylian prince and Nestor's brother, was killed by Hercules. The speaker's lineage is boasted to shame the brother into fighting.
The Dawn-queen is Eos, Memnon's mother, who divinely deflects the spears from her son.
"Nought recking" means paying no heed; Memnon disregards Thrasymedes and Phereus as weaklings.
"Weened" is archaic for thought or supposed.
"Of sore need" means because I am forced to; Memnon would kill Nestor only reluctantly.
"The son of Neleus" is Nestor's son, Thrasymedes, identified by his grandfather's name; Nestor himself is Neleus's son.
"Brocket" is a young male deer; "hind" is a female red deer; "giving tongue" means hounds barking on the scent.
Aeacus' son is Peleus, Achilles' father; so Achilles is Aeacus' grandson, and the text uses 'son' loosely for descendant in sentence 166 too.
'Corse' means corpse; 'I fear me lest' means 'I fear that'.
'Forthright' means straight away; 'wroth' means angry.
'I trow' means 'I believe'; 'dark doom' is his appointed death.
The Hesperid Maids were nymphs of the far west who guarded the golden apples; Memnon claims they raised him by the Ocean river.
Alludes to the myth that Dionysus fled King Lycurgus and took refuge with Thetis in the sea.
The 'God-smith' is Hephaestus, who was hurled from heaven and sheltered by Thetis and Eurynome.
The 'Lightning-lord' is Zeus; Thetis was said to have saved him when other gods bound him, by summoning the hundred-handed giant.
The Goat-star (Capella) rises with storms, so sailors feared the sea; the comparison likens the dead-hidden earth to a clouded sky.
The 'silver cord of life' pictures life as a thread or cord that is cut at death.
"Palled" means wrapped or covered, as with a funeral pall (cloth over a coffin).
"Hest" is an archaic word for command.
Paphlagoneion is a river named for Paphlagonia, in northern Asia Minor; the passage presents it as made from Memnon's blood-drops.
"Reek" means foul smell; "humours" are bodily fluids, here pus or corrupt matter from a wound.
Aesopus is a river near Troy; its daughters are river nymphs who plant trees around Memnon's grave mound (barrow).
"Cronos' Son" is Zeus; Dawn threatens to leave the world in primal Chaos until he feels her pain.
Nereus' Child is Thetis, the sea-goddess and mother of Achilles, who killed Memnon. Dawn resents her son's death while Thetis's son is honoured.
The "Memnons" are birds said to fight yearly at his tomb, a legend explaining their origin.
"Dree their weird" is archaic: endure their fate.

context_notes.text: Thymoetes is an elderly Trojan counsellor. Hector, Troy's greatest defender, has just been killed by Achilles.
Priam, son of Laomedon, is the aged king of Troy, here called by his father's name.
Polydamas is a Trojan noble, known for prudence; he had long advised caution and returning Helen.
The Trojans fear Paris, whose abduction of Helen caused the war, and Helen herself, so none will say openly that she should be returned.
Laomedon's son is Priam, king of Troy, who hopes Memnon will turn the war against the Greek ships.
Memnon is the son of Eos, goddess of the Dawn, and Tithonus. He is fated to be killed by Achilles.
Hephaestus was the divine smith of the gods; Zeus gave him Aphrodite as bride.
Zeus, son of Cronos, rules the gods and knows the fates. Here he foresees heavy slaughter the next day.
Peleus' son is Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior, in whom the Argives (Greeks) put their trust.
Nestor, son of Neleus, is the aged Greek counsellor from Pylos; Antilochus is his son.
The old man is Nestor, king of Pylos, whose son Antilochus Memnon has just killed. Memnon honours his age.
The Hellespont is the strait near Troy; the Greek ships and camp lay on its shore.
Memnon, king of the Ethiopians (Aethiops), came to aid Troy; his men are the Aethiop hands.
Nestor is the aged Greek counsellor; his son Antilochus has just been killed by Memnon.
Memnon, king of the Ethiopians, is son of Eos, goddess of Dawn, and Tithonus; he came to aid Troy.
The Fates were the goddesses who spun and decided each mortal's destiny; their arrival signals who must die.
Enyo is a goddess of war, here prolonging the evenly matched struggle.
The Aethiopians were Memnon's followers, who came with him to fight for Troy.
The twelve maidens are the Hours, goddesses of the seasons and the ordered round of the year.
The Pleiads are the seven star-sisters, daughters of Atlas, here joining the mourning.
Antilochus, Nestor's son, was a Greek killed earlier in the battle, so the Argives mourn him while praising Achilles.

literary_notes.text: The Trojans' dread of Achilles leaping the wall in one bound shows how his terror has grown larger than life.
Thymoetes remembers hoping Penthesileia was a divine saviour, yet she fell, deepening the sense of doom.
Priam's choice of honourable death over shameful exile shows his dignity and stubborn hope.
Paris's stacked insults and sarcasm reveal his defensive pride and his need to deflect blame.
Polydamas turns Paris's boast of valour around, showing it as reckless selfishness that will ruin Troy.
Paris's silence reveals his guilt, and the narrator notes the Trojans are already watching for the Argives he provoked.
Storm-worn sailors glimpsing the guiding stars compare to Trojans seeing Memnon: he is their hope of rescue.
This terse line hints that Priam's line will end, and the heirloom will not pass to his son.
Memnon's modest refusal to boast contrasts with Priam's hopeful flattery and shows his restraint.
"His last!" is a narrator's interjection announcing Memnon's coming death.
Sleep is imagined as a gentle being sliding down upon the sleepers.
Sleep is a gentle figure who spreads veils over the gods' eyes, softening their grief.
The rushing army is compared to storm clouds herded across the sky, suggesting darkness and menace.
Comparing the army to locusts stresses its vast numbers and the famine it will bring.
Achilles is likened to a giant Titan, emphasising his size and pride.
"Firstfruits of death's harvest" casts killing as reaping, a recurring battle image.
Memnon leaping at Antilochus is likened to a fearless lion attacking a boar.
The narrator's general reflection on a father's grief deepens sympathy for Nestor.
Memnon is compared to a boar or bear turning on hunters, showing his fierce defiance against two attackers.
Memnon as a lion over a kill and the Greeks as timid jackals shows his dominance.
Nestor likens himself to a toothless old lion driven off by a cur, expressing the pathos of age.
An extended storm-flood simile conveys Memnon's overwhelming, noisy sweep through the Argives.
Doom stands beside Memnon smiling and flattering him, foreshadowing his coming death.
The falling crag, hurled by Zeus, makes Memnon's attack a natural catastrophe that scatters the Greeks.
Memnon's scorn of Thetis as obscure and deedless is undercut by Achilles' reply, which lists her great deeds for the gods.
The dust cloud is compared to mist and flooding torrents that terrify shepherds, conveying the scale and menace of the fight.
The dark Fate shadowing Memnon and the bright one haloing Achilles use light and dark to foreshadow the outcome.
The heroes are likened to storm-battered headlands, stressing their immovable endurance.
Trampled corpses are compared to fallen autumn leaves underfoot, making the carnage seem a natural, mournful waste.
Achilles pursuing the Trojans is likened to a destructive whirlwind, ending the scene on his unstoppable power.
The world shares the goddess's grief: her clouds darken the earth.
The mourning Aethiopians are compared to a hunter's friends and hounds carrying his body from a fatal hunt.
The Hours dance as maidens at heaven's doors, turning the seasons into a living image.
Dawn addresses her dead son directly, making her grief immediate.
Dawn's endless tears are likened to a brimming river, showing immortal grief on a vast scale.
Dawn's fear of Zeus' threat prepares her return to her daily course, restoring cosmic order.
